prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) -- Afghan lawmakers have directly accused Pakistan's intelligence agency of involvement in a string of deadly attacks in Afghanistan, blasting their neighbor as "the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism." The recent attack by a suicide bomber on the Indian embassy in Kabul killed more than 40 people. A Pakistani official Tuesday bristled at the accusation, saying that Afghan lawmakers were making allegations without proof. "We are not an irresponsible nation and we don't blame our failures on others," said a senior official with Pakistan's Directorate for Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI). "If they want to engage in this kind of game, let them be." The Afghan Cabinet made the scathing indictment in a resolution Monday, saying Afghanistan would boycott a series of meetings with Pakistan unless "bilateral trust" is restored. In recent weeks a wave of attacks carried out by Islamic militants have killed scores of people in Afghanistan, including an assault on a military outpost Sunday that killed nine U.S. soldiers, as well as a suicide attack on the Indian Embassy a week ago that killed 58 people. The two incidents, along with an assassination attempt against Afghan President Hamid Karzai at a military ceremony on April 27, are "indicative of the attempts by the ISI (Inter-Services Intelligence) to once again occupy Afghanistan and to perish the true right of the people of Afghanistan for national sovereignty," the resolution said. Afghanistan regularly accuses Pakistan's intelligence service -- which once had strong ties with the Taliban -- of orchestrating attacks inside its borders. Pakistan has repeatedly denied involvement, including in the incidents that the resolution cited. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates also said there is no indication that "foreign agents" were responsible for the embassy attack. The senior ISI official said Tuesday that if Afghanistan has proof that Pakistani intelligence agents were involved in the attacks, that proof should be presented and the ISI will act on it. The official said that the Pakistani government could also blame incidents in Pakistan, like recent attacks in Karachi and Hangu, on others. But without proof, he said, it would be irresponsible. Pakistan and Afghanistan have a tumultuous history that dates back several years. During the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, religious schools in Pakistan helped train fighters who battled the Soviets. After the Taliban took over Afghanistan in 1996 and imposed fundamentalist rule, Pakistan was one of the few countries that recognized the regime diplomatically. It dropped its support after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in Washington and New York. But Afghanistan claims that Pakistan continues to informally support the militants, who operate from havens in Pakistan's lawless tribal regions near the porous 1,500-mile border the two countries share. Adding fresh ammunition to the suspicions, the Rand Corp. -- a U.S. think tank -- released a report last month that said some members of Pakistan's intelligence service and its paramilitary corps were helping insurgents in Afghanistan. The study, funded by the U.S. Defense Department, alleged that members of the two agencies often tipped off militants to the location and movement of coalition forces trying to rout them. It also said personnel within the agencies trained fighters at camps in Pakistan, financed them and helped them cross the border into Afghanistan. The Pakistani military denied and denounced the report, calling it a "smear campaign" designed to "create doubts and suspicion in the minds of (the) target audience." Relations between the two countries are strained to such a point that Karzai has threatened to send troops across the border to take on the militants. "The people of Afghanistan and the international community have come to the reality that Pakistan intelligence institutions and its army have become the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism and extremism to the world and particularly to Afghanistan," Monday's resolution said.

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) — Afghan legislators have openly charged Pakistan’s intelligence service with helping carry out a series of lethal attacks in Afghanistan, describing the neighboring country as “the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism.”

A suicide bombing at India’s embassy in Kabul recently left more than 40 people dead. On Tuesday, a Pakistani official sharply rejected the claims, arguing that Afghan lawmakers had offered no evidence.

“We are not an irresponsible nation and we don't blame our failures on others,” said a senior official from Pakistan’s Directorate for Inter-Services Intelligence, or ISI. “If they want to engage in this kind of game, let them be.”

The accusations appeared in a strongly worded resolution adopted Monday by Afghanistan’s Cabinet. The measure said Afghanistan would stay away from several meetings with Pakistan until “bilateral trust” had been re-established.

Scores of people have died in Afghanistan during a recent surge of attacks by Islamic militants. Nine U.S. troops were killed Sunday when a military outpost came under assault, while a suicide bombing at the Indian Embassy a week earlier claimed 58 lives.

According to the resolution, those two attacks—together with the April 27 attempt to assassinate Afghan President Hamid Karzai during a military ceremony—showed that the ISI was trying “to once again occupy Afghanistan and to perish the true right of the people of Afghanistan for national sovereignty.”

Afghan authorities have frequently alleged that Pakistan’s intelligence agency, which previously maintained close relations with the Taliban, has organized attacks on Afghan soil. Pakistan has consistently denied such involvement, including any role in the incidents named in the resolution.

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates also said there was no evidence that “foreign agents” were behind the embassy bombing.

The senior ISI official said Tuesday that Afghanistan should provide any proof it possesses linking Pakistani intelligence personnel to the violence, adding that the agency would respond to credible evidence. He noted that Pakistan could similarly accuse outsiders of responsibility for recent incidents in places such as Karachi and Hangu, but said doing so without evidence would be irresponsible.

Afghanistan and Pakistan have had a troubled relationship stretching back years. During the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, religious schools in Pakistan assisted in training combatants who fought Soviet forces. When the Taliban seized control of Afghanistan in 1996 and introduced a fundamentalist system of government, Pakistan became one of only a small number of countries to grant the regime diplomatic recognition.

Pakistan ended that backing following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in New York and Washington. Afghanistan, however, maintains that Pakistan still provides unofficial assistance to militants based in safe havens within Pakistan’s largely ungoverned tribal areas near the countries’ porous, 1,500-mile frontier.

Those suspicions were reinforced last month by a report from the Rand Corp., a U.S. think tank. The study concluded that certain members of Pakistan’s intelligence agency and paramilitary forces were assisting insurgents operating in Afghanistan.

Funded by the U.S. Defense Department, the report alleged that personnel from both organizations regularly warned militants about the positions and movements of coalition troops attempting to defeat them. It further claimed that agency members trained fighters in Pakistani camps, supplied them with money and helped them enter Afghanistan across the border.

Pakistan’s military condemned and rejected the findings, characterizing the report as a “smear campaign” intended to “create doubts and suspicion in the minds of (the) target audience.”

Tensions between Kabul and Islamabad have grown so severe that Karzai has threatened to deploy Afghan forces across the frontier to confront the militants.

“The people of Afghanistan and the international community have come to the reality that Pakistan intelligence institutions and its army have become the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism and extremism to the world and particularly to Afghanistan,” the Afghan resolution stated.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Afghan lawmakers accusing Pakistan’s ISI of involvement in deadly militant attacks, including the Kabul Indian Embassy bombing and Pakistan’s response.
counterfactuals.output:
**Afghan lawmakers accuse Pakistan spy agency over deadly attacks**

**KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN)** — Afghan lawmakers accused Pakistan’s powerful Inter-Services Intelligence agency of supporting a series of militant attacks in Afghanistan, including the suicide bombing outside the Indian Embassy in Kabul that killed more than 40 people.

Members of Afghanistan’s parliament said the scale and coordination of the violence suggested involvement by a foreign intelligence service. They cited the embassy bombing, an attempt to assassinate President Hamid Karzai and other major Taliban operations as evidence of alleged interference by Pakistan’s ISI.

Pakistan rejected the accusations, calling them unsubstantiated and demanding that Afghanistan provide evidence.

The car bomb outside the Indian Embassy exploded during the morning rush hour on July 7, 2008, as people lined up for visas and employees entered the diplomatic compound. Among those killed were an Indian diplomat and India’s defense attaché. More than 100 people were wounded.

Afghan officials said the attack had been planned outside the country and alleged that Pakistan’s intelligence service played a role. India also said the bombing bore the hallmarks of forces seeking to undermine its relationship with Afghanistan, though Pakistani officials denied any involvement.

Islamabad condemned the bombing and said it was prepared to cooperate with Afghan and Indian authorities in an investigation. Pakistani officials described allegations against the ISI as an attempt to blame Pakistan for Afghanistan’s worsening security problems.

Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have long been strained by accusations that Taliban and other militant groups operate from sanctuaries in Pakistan’s tribal regions. Kabul has repeatedly charged that elements within Pakistan’s security establishment support insurgents crossing the border.

Pakistan says it is itself a victim of terrorism and has deployed troops against militants near the Afghan frontier. It has also accused Kabul of failing to prevent anti-Pakistan fighters from using Afghan territory.

The dispute deepened regional tensions at a time when Taliban attacks were increasing across Afghanistan and international forces were struggling to contain the insurgency.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the escalating diplomatic tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan in 2008, focusing on allegations that the ISI supported Taliban attacks.
counterfactuals.output:
Afghanistan–Pakistan relations deteriorated sharply in 2008 as Kabul increasingly accused Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence agency (ISI) of helping Taliban and Haqqani-network militants conduct attacks inside Afghanistan.

- After the April 2008 attack on a military parade in Kabul—an apparent attempt to assassinate President Hamid Karzai—Afghan officials said the plotters had links to Pakistan-based militants and alleged ISI involvement. Pakistan rejected the charge.
- Tensions rose further as Karzai accused Pakistan of allowing Taliban leaders and training bases to operate across the border. In June, he threatened to send Afghan forces into Pakistan to pursue figures such as Mullah Omar and Baitullah Mehsud, prompting strong Pakistani protests over sovereignty.
- The decisive rupture came after the July 7 bombing of the Indian Embassy in Kabul, which killed more than 50 people. Afghan authorities publicly blamed the ISI, arguing that the attack bore the hallmarks of a professional intelligence operation. India made similar allegations, and U.S. intelligence reportedly found evidence connecting ISI elements to the Haqqani network, which was blamed for the bombing.
- Pakistan denied directing or supporting the attacks, called the accusations unsubstantiated, and emphasized its own losses in fighting militants. It also offered cooperation or investigation while warning Kabul against inflammatory claims.

By late 2008, the dispute had become more than a recurring border quarrel: Afghanistan portrayed the insurgency as sustained by elements of the Pakistani state, while Pakistan maintained that Kabul was scapegoating it for Afghanistan’s internal security failures. The mutual accusations undermined intelligence-sharing, border cooperation, and broader efforts to combat the Taliban.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a detailed international news story covering Afghanistan’s threat to boycott meetings with Pakistan after lawmakers blamed Pakistani intelligence for recent attacks.
counterfactuals.output:
**Afghanistan threatens to boycott talks with Pakistan as lawmakers blame intelligence service for attacks**

**KABUL** — Afghanistan has threatened to boycott future meetings with Pakistan unless Islamabad takes concrete action against militant groups operating from its territory, deepening a diplomatic crisis after Afghan lawmakers accused Pakistan’s intelligence service of involvement in a series of recent attacks.

During heated parliamentary debate in Kabul, several lawmakers alleged that Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, or ISI, had supported or sheltered networks responsible for violence in Afghanistan. They called on the Afghan government to suspend official contacts with Islamabad and reconsider security cooperation until Pakistan demonstrates that it is dismantling militant sanctuaries.

The accusations came amid renewed public anger over attacks that killed and wounded civilians and members of Afghanistan’s security forces. Afghan officials have long blamed elements of the Taliban and the Haqqani network for major assaults, arguing that their leaders and logistical networks have benefited from safe havens across the border.

Pakistan has repeatedly rejected allegations that it sponsors violence in Afghanistan. Pakistani officials say their country has suffered heavily from terrorism, has conducted extensive military operations against armed groups and wants a stable Afghan state. Islamabad has also accused Kabul of allowing militants hostile to Pakistan to operate from Afghan territory.

The Afghan boycott threat could affect bilateral political and security meetings intended to address border management, intelligence sharing, refugee issues, trade and efforts to revive peace negotiations. Afghan officials did not immediately specify whether all contacts would be suspended or whether essential diplomatic and technical channels would remain open.

Lawmakers said continued meetings would have little value without measurable results.

“Dialogue cannot continue simply for appearances while Afghan citizens are being killed,” one legislator said during the debate, reflecting a broader demand for Kabul to adopt a tougher policy toward its eastern neighbor.

The allegations against the ISI were not accompanied by publicly released evidence, and responsibility for individual attacks is often difficult to establish independently. Militant organizations have sometimes claimed attacks directly, while in other cases Afghan authorities have based their accusations on intelligence assessments that remain classified.

Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have been strained for years by mutual mistrust and a disputed frontier. Kabul argues that Islamabad has distinguished between militant groups that threaten Pakistan and those focused on Afghanistan. Pakistan denies that charge and says Afghan instability, weak border controls and the presence of anti-Pakistan fighters inside Afghanistan pose direct threats to its security.

The roughly 2,600-kilometer border between the countries cuts through remote and mountainous terrain and divides Pashtun communities on both sides. Pakistan recognizes the frontier as an international border and has built fencing along much of it, while Afghanistan has historically disputed the boundary’s legitimacy.

Despite the acrimony, the two countries remain closely linked. Pakistan is a major trade and transit route for landlocked Afghanistan and hosts a large Afghan refugee population. Afghan and Pakistani officials also need to coordinate on customs, cross-border movement and security incidents, making a complete diplomatic rupture costly for both sides.

Regional governments and international partners are likely to press Kabul and Islamabad to maintain communication. Previous periods of heightened tension have led to border closures, disruptions to commerce and retaliatory accusations, but have generally been followed by renewed talks under international mediation.

Analysts said a boycott could increase pressure on Pakistan in the short term but might also remove one of the few mechanisms available for resolving disputes.

“The central problem is not the absence of meetings but the absence of trust,” said a Kabul-based political analyst. “Afghanistan wants action against the groups it believes are planning attacks from Pakistan, while Pakistan wants stronger measures against militants it says are based in Afghanistan. Without credible verification, both sides return to the same cycle of accusation and denial.”

Afghan authorities are under intense domestic pressure to explain security failures and prevent further violence. Families of victims and members of parliament have demanded investigations into how attackers obtained weapons, crossed security checkpoints and reached heavily guarded targets.

Pakistan, meanwhile, has urged Afghanistan to share evidence through established diplomatic and intelligence channels rather than making accusations in public. It has said cooperation, not confrontation, is the only sustainable response to militant violence affecting both countries.

It remained unclear whether Kabul would carry out the boycott threat or use it as leverage ahead of the next scheduled round of discussions. But the dispute underscored how quickly attacks inside Afghanistan can spill into an already fragile relationship—complicating counterterrorism efforts, regional trade and attempts to build a broader political settlement.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain Afghanistan’s accusations against Pakistan’s intelligence service, citing the Indian Embassy bombing, the attack that killed nine U.S. soldiers, the attempt on Hamid Karzai, and the RAND Corporation report.
counterfactuals.output:
Afghanistan’s accusations centered on the claim that elements of Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence Directorate (ISI) were covertly supporting Taliban and Haqqani-network militants while Pakistan publicly presented itself as an ally against terrorism.

- **Indian Embassy bombing, Kabul, 7 July 2008:** A suicide car bomb killed more than 50 people, including Indian diplomats. Afghan officials blamed the ISI, arguing that Pakistan wanted to curb India’s growing influence in Afghanistan. U.S. intelligence officials later said intercepted communications indicated that ISI officers had helped plan the bombing. Pakistan denied involvement.

- **Attack that killed nine U.S. soldiers, 13 July 2008:** Taliban fighters assaulted a U.S. outpost at Wanat in Kunar Province, near the Pakistani border, killing nine American soldiers. Afghan officials cited the attack as evidence that insurgents could organize, train, and obtain assistance from sanctuaries inside Pakistan. The attack itself did not conclusively prove direct ISI control, but it reinforced Kabul’s allegation that Pakistani security institutions tolerated or assisted cross-border militant networks.

- **Attempt to kill President Hamid Karzai, 27 April 2008:** Taliban gunmen attacked a military parade in Kabul attended by Karzai. He escaped, but several people were killed. Afghan investigators said the plot was connected to militants operating from Pakistan and alleged involvement by a foreign intelligence service—widely understood as a reference to the ISI. Pakistan again rejected the charge.

- **RAND Corporation report:** A RAND study on the Afghan insurgency reported that Taliban and other insurgent groups benefited from sanctuary, recruitment, logistics, intelligence, and other assistance in Pakistan. It stated that some members of the ISI and Pakistan’s Frontier Corps appeared to provide support to insurgents, although it did not necessarily portray all such activity as an officially unified policy of the Pakistani state.

Taken together, Kabul’s case was that these were not isolated attacks: they reflected a broader system in which militant groups used Pakistani territory and allegedly received help from parts of Pakistan’s security establishment. Pakistan maintained that it was itself a victim of terrorism, denied directing the attacks, and argued that Afghanistan was blaming it for failures of security and governance inside Afghanistan.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
